description: A seventh Level 1 - Math I (Physics) exam set covering advanced calculus techniques, complex roots, convergence, vector spaces and bases, parameter systems, and diagonalisation.
instructions: All main questions carry the same number of marks.
Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Begin each main question on a new page.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: This question concerns product differentiation, higher-order limiting behaviour, squeeze arguments, and implicit differentiation.
questions.title: Differentiation and oscillatory limits

parts.answer: Use the expansion \(\sin u=u-u^3/6+O(u^5)\). With \(u=4x\), \(\sin(4x)-4x=-(4x)^3/6+O(x^5)\). Dividing by \(x^3\) gives the limit \(-64/6=-32/3\).
parts.label: (b)

parts.answer: Since \(-1\le\cos(2/x)\le1\), and \(|x^3|\to0\), we have \(-|x|^3\le x^3\cos(2/x)\le |x|^3\). Both outer bounds tend to \(0\). By the squeeze theorem, the limit is \(0\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use the squeeze theorem to evaluate \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to0}x^3\cos(2/x)\).

parts.answer: Differentiate \(e^y+xy=e\) with respect to \(x\). This gives \(e^y y'+y+xy'=0\). Collecting \(y'\) terms gives \((e^y+x)y'=-y\), so \(y'=-y/(e^y+x)\). At \((0,1)\), \(y'=-1/e\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: For the curve \(e^y+xy=e\), find \(dy/dx\) and evaluate it at \((0,1)\).

questions.stem: This question uses trigonometric substitution, logarithmic substitution, and repeated integration by parts.
questions.title: Integration by method selection

parts.answer: Let \(u=\cos x\), so \(du=-\sin x\,dx\). Then \(\int\cos^5x\sin x\,dx=-\int u^5\,du=-u^6/6+C\). Substituting back gives \(-\cos^6x/6+C\).
parts.label: (a)

parts.answer: Let \(u=1+x^3\), so \(du=3x^2\,dx\). The bounds are \(u=1\) and \(u=2\). Therefore \(\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx=\frac13\int_1^2\frac{du}{u}=\frac13\ln2\).
parts.label: (b)

parts.answer: Let \(I=\int e^x\cos x\,dx\). Integrate by parts with \(u=\cos x\), \(dv=e^x dx\), giving \(I=e^x\cos x+\int e^x\sin x\,dx\). Let \(J=\int e^x\sin x\,dx\). Then \(J=e^x\sin x-I\). Hence \(I=e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x-I\), so \(2I=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)\). Therefore \(I=\frac{e^x(\sin x+\cos x)}{2}+C\).
parts.label: (c)

questions.stem: This question concerns polar form, roots, and exponential equations.
questions.title: Complex roots and exponential form

parts.answer: The modulus is \(\sqrt{2^2+(-2\sqrt3)^2}=4\). The point is in the fourth quadrant with reference angle \(\pi/3\), so the principal argument is \(-\pi/3\). Hence \(2-2\sqrt3\,i=4e^{-i\pi/3}\).
parts.label: (a)

parts.answer: Write \(32=32e^{2\pi i k}\). The fifth roots have modulus \(32^{1/5}=2\), and arguments \(2\pi k/5\), for \(k=0,1,2,3,4\). Therefore the roots are \(2e^{2\pi i k/5}\), where \(k=0,1,2,3,4\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find all fifth roots of \(32\), giving the roots in exponential form.

parts.answer: Using \(\cos z=(e^{iz}+e^{-iz})/2\), set \(z=ib\). Then \(e^{iz}=e^{-b}\) and \(e^{-iz}=e^b\). Hence \(\cos(ib)=\frac{e^{-b}+e^b}{2}=\cosh b\).
parts.label: (c)

parts.answer: Write \(z=x+iy\). Then \(e^{2z}=e^{2x}e^{2iy}\), and \(4i=4e^{i(\pi/2+2k\pi)}\). Matching moduli gives \(e^{2x}=4\), so \(x=\ln2\). Matching arguments gives \(2y=\pi/2+2k\pi\), so \(y=\pi/4+k\pi\). Thus \(z=\ln2+i(\pi/4+k\pi)\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
parts.label: (d)

questions.stem: This question covers comparison tests, conditional convergence, geometric comparison, and power-series endpoints.
questions.title: Convergence and intervals

parts.answer: Use limit comparison with \(1/n^{3/2}\). Since \(\frac{1/\sqrt{n^3+1}}{1/n^{3/2}}=\sqrt{\frac{n^3}{n^3+1}}\to1\), and \(\sum1/n^{3/2}\) converges, the given series converges.
parts.label: (a)

parts.answer: The magnitudes are \(n/(n^2+4)\), which tend to \(0\) and decrease eventually. The alternating series test gives convergence. For absolute convergence, \(\frac{n/(n^2+4)}{1/n}=\frac{n^2}{n^2+4}\to1\), so the absolute-value series diverges like the harmonic series. Therefore the original series is conditionally convergent.
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Determine whether \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{n}{n^2+4}\) is absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.

parts.answer: For every \(n\), \(0<\frac{4^n}{n^2 5^n}=\frac{1}{n^2}(4/5)^n\le(4/5)^n\). Since the geometric series \(\sum(4/5)^n\) converges, the comparison test shows the given series converges.
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use comparison to show that \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{4^n}{n^2 5^n}\) converges.

parts.answer: Use the root test: \(\sqrt[n]{|n(x+1)^n/4^n|}=n^{1/n}|x+1|/4\to|x+1|/4\). The interior condition is \(|x+1|<4\), so \(-5<x<3\). At \(x=3\), the terms are \(n\), and at \(x=-5\), the terms are \(n(-1)^n\); neither tends to zero. The interval is \((-5,3)\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n(x+1)^n}{4^n}\).

questions.section: Section E: Vector Spaces and Bases
questions.title: Span, bases, dimension, and coordinates

parts.answer: Compute \(u_1+u_2=(1,0,1)+(0,1,1)=(1,1,2)=u_3\). Thus \(u_1+u_2-u_3=\mathbf0\) is a non-trivial linear relation. Therefore \(u_3\) is linearly dependent on \(u_1\) and \(u_2\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that \(u_3\) is linearly dependent on \(u_1\) and \(u_2\).

parts.answer: The vectors \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) are independent: if \(a u_1+b u_2=\mathbf0\), then \((a,b,a+b)=(0,0,0)\), so \(a=0\) and \(b=0\). Part (a) shows that \(u_3\) adds no new direction because \(u_3=u_1+u_2\). Hence \(\{u_1,u_2\}\) is a basis for \(\operatorname{span}\{u_1,u_2,u_3\}\).
parts.label: (b)

parts.answer: A general linear combination of \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) is \(a u_1+b u_2=(a,b,a+b)\). Such a vector satisfies \(x+y-z=a+b-(a+b)=0\), so the span is contained in \(W\). Conversely, if \((x,y,z)\in W\), then \(x+y-z=0\), so \(z=x+y\). Hence \((x,y,z)=(x,y,x+y)=x u_1+y u_2\), which lies in the span. Therefore \(\operatorname{span}\{u_1,u_2,u_3\}=W\), and \(\dim W=2\).
parts.label: (c)

parts.answer: Solve \(a u_1+b u_2=(2,-1,1)\). Since \(a u_1+b u_2=(a,b,a+b)\), comparing components gives \(a=2\), \(b=-1\), and \(a+b=1\), which is consistent. Therefore the coordinates of \((2,-1,1)\) in the ordered basis \((u_1,u_2)\) are \((2,-1)\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of \((2,-1,1)\) in the ordered basis \((u_1,u_2)\).

questions.stem:
Consider the parameter-dependent system
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+y+2z&=4,\\
2x+3y+5z&=9,\\
x+ay+3z&=b.
\end{aligned}
\]
questions.title: Parameter classification by row reduction

parts.answer: The coefficient determinant is \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\2&3&5\\1&a&3\end{pmatrix}=2-a\). Therefore the coefficient matrix is invertible and the system has a unique solution exactly when \(a\ne2\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the values of \(a\) for which the system has a unique solution.

parts.answer: Row reduction gives \(R_2-2R_1=(0,1,1|1)\) and \(R_3-R_1=(0,a-1,1|b-4)\). Replacing \(R_3\) by \(R_3-(a-1)R_2\) gives \((0,0,2-a|b-a-3)\). When \(a=2\), this becomes \((0,0,0|b-5)\). If \(b\ne5\), there is no solution. If \(b=5\), there are infinitely many solutions.
parts.label: (b)

parts.answer: For \(a=2\) and \(b=5\), the reduced equations are \(x+y+2z=4\) and \(y+z=1\). Let \(z=t\). Then \(y=1-t\), and \(x=4-(1-t)-2t=3-t\). Hence \((x,y,z)=(3-t,1-t,t)\), where \(t\in\mathbb R\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For the infinitely many solution case, write the solution set in parameter form.

parts.answer: For \(a=1\), \(b=4\), the last row coefficient is \(2-a=1\), and the right-hand side is \(b-a-3=0\), so \(z=0\). Then \(y+z=1\) gives \(y=1\), and \(x+y+2z=4\) gives \(x=3\). The solution is \((3,1,0)\).
parts.label: (d)

questions.section: Section G: Eigenvalues and Matrix Structure
questions.title: Diagonalising a two-dimensional map

parts.answer: The characteristic polynomial is \(\det(A-\lambda I)=\det\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda&1\\-2&3-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=\lambda^2-3\lambda+2\). Hence \(\lambda=1\) or \(\lambda=2\).
parts.label: (a)

parts.answer: For \(\lambda=1\), \((A-I)\mathbf v=0\) gives an eigenvector \((1,1)^T\). For \(\lambda=2\), \((A-2I)\mathbf v=0\) gives \((1,2)^T\). Thus \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(D=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\). Since \(\det P=1\ne0\), \(A=PDP^{-1}\).
parts.label: (b)

parts.answer: Here \(P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\), so \(A^n=P\operatorname{diag}(1,2^n)P^{-1}\). Multiplying gives \(A^n=\begin{pmatrix}2-2^n&-1+2^n\\2-2^{n+1}&-1+2^{n+1}\end{pmatrix}\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use the diagonalisation to find a formula for \(A^n\), where \(n\) is a positive integer.

parts.answer: The statement is false. A repeated eigenvalue does not by itself prevent diagonalisation. For example, \(I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has repeated eigenvalue \(1\), but every non-zero vector is an eigenvector, so it has two independent eigenvectors and is diagonalizable.
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Decide whether the statement is true or false, with justification: every matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is not diagonalizable.
